blocks.text: Registering a tool is the moment a server developer actually hands a capability over to the SDK. Up to this point a tool is just an idea, after registration it is a real thing a model can discover and call.
The SDK asks for four things when you register a tool, a name, a description, an input schema, and a handler function that does the real work.

This lesson walks through registering a tool in both the TypeScript and Python SDKs, keeping the schema and the handler honest with each other, organizing dozens of tools without one file spiraling out of control, and testing that a registered tool actually behaves.
1. What Registering a Tool Actually Means

blocks.alt: What Registering a Tool Actually Means
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804557-507496157.png

When you register a tool, you are calling one SDK method that does two separate jobs at once. It stores metadata that the server can answer tools/list with, and it wires up a function that runs when tools/call arrives for that name.
Nothing about a tool is real to the outside world until this call happens. A handler sitting in your codebase unregistered is just a normal function, invisible to any model.
Most SDKs expose this as a single method call, which is a deliberate design choice, it makes it much harder to accidentally publish a description without the handler that backs it up.

blocks.title: One call, two jobs
blocks.content: Registration publishes the tool description for discovery and connects the handler for execution. Both come from the same registration call, which is exactly why keeping them together matters so much.

blocks.text: 2. The Four Pieces Every Registration Needs

blocks.alt: The Four Pieces Every Registration Needs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012144-837370844.png
Every tool registration, regardless of SDK or language, boils down to the same four ingredients.

items: Name: a short, unique, machine friendly identifier the model uses in every tools/call request.
Description: plain language explaining what the tool does and when a model should reach for it.
Input schema: the JSON Schema describing exactly which arguments are valid.
Handler: the actual function that runs when a call comes in and produces a result.

blocks.text: Miss any one of these and the tool either will not register, will not be discoverable in a useful way, or will not actually do anything when called.
3. Registering a Tool With the TypeScript SDK
The TypeScript SDK exposes a server.tool method that takes the name, description, a schema built with a validation library like zod, and the handler, all in one call.

Notice the schema is written once, as zod fields, and the handler receives already parsed arguments matching that same shape. The SDK validates the incoming call against the schema before your handler ever runs.
The order of arguments to server.tool matters, name first, then description, then schema, then handler, and getting that order wrong is a surprisingly common early mistake.
4. Registering a Tool With the Python SDK
The Python SDK, through FastMCP, takes a different shape but registers the exact same four pieces. A decorator marks a plain function as a tool.

code.content:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("weather-server")

@mcp.tool()
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the current weather for a named city"""
    data = fetch_weather(city)
    return "Weather in " + city + ": " + data.summary

blocks.text: Here the input schema is generated automatically from the function signature and type hints, and the description comes straight from the docstring. Same four pieces, far less boilerplate to write by hand.
This is a good moment to stop and notice that both SDKs are solving the exact same problem, they just choose different amounts of automation for turning your intent into a JSON Schema.
5. The Handler Function Contract
A handler receives one argument, the parsed and already validated input object, and it returns a result the SDK can package into a tools/call response.
A handler should never assume it needs to re check basic types or required fields itself. Validation against the schema already happened before the handler was invoked.

blocks.text: 6. Shaping the Return Value
A handler in the TypeScript SDK returns an object with a content array, usually one text block, though a tool can return multiple content items.
In the Python SDK a plain return value like a string is enough, FastMCP wraps it into the right content shape automatically before it reaches the client.
7. Handling Errors Inside a Handler
A handler should catch its own failures and return them as a normal, structured error result rather than letting an unhandled exception crash the request.
An isError result still shows up as a normal tools/call response, it just tells the model the attempt failed, so the model can decide what to try next instead of the whole exchange breaking.
8. Why Schema and Handler Must Describe the Same Thing

blocks.alt: Why Schema and Handler Must Describe the Same Thing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-227290037.png

The schema is a promise made to the model about what arguments are valid. The handler is the code that actually reads those arguments. If the two disagree, the promise is broken even though nothing crashes.
A model only ever sees the schema, never the handler body. Whatever the schema claims is true, as far as the model is concerned, regardless of what the handler actually does with it.

blocks.title: Trust boundary
blocks.content: The schema is the only thing a model can read. Every quiet mismatch between schema and handler becomes a call that looks correct to the model yet behaves wrong on the server.

blocks.text: 9. A Drift Example: When Schema and Handler Disagree

blocks.alt: A Drift Example: When Schema and Handler Disagree
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-694405599.png
Imagine a tool originally took a single units field. Later the developer renames the internal variable to unit but forgets to update the schema.

Every call looks perfectly valid to the model and passes schema validation, yet the handler silently ignores the value it actually needed. This is exactly the kind of bug that only shows up when someone tests real behavior, not just discovery.
10. Keeping Schema and Handler in Sync as a Tool Evolves
The safest habit is to treat the schema and the handler as one unit that only ever changes together, never as two files edited on different days.

items: Rename a field in the schema and the handler destructuring in the same commit, never one without the other.
When adding a new required field, update example calls and any tests in the same change.
When a field becomes optional, check the handler actually has a sensible fallback for it being missing.
Prefer generating the schema from the same types the handler uses, so drift becomes a compile error instead of a silent bug.

blocks.text: That last point is why the Python SDK generating a schema straight from type hints is such a strong pattern, the schema simply cannot drift from the function signature because it is derived from it.
11. Organizing Many Tools Without One Giant File
A server with three tools can live comfortably in one file. A server with thirty tools in one file becomes a file nobody wants to open.
The fix is simple, give each tool its own small file that exports its name, description, schema, and handler together, since those four pieces belong together anyway.
12. A Central Registry That Collects Every Tool

blocks.alt: A Central Registry That Collects Every Tool
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-965173303.png
One small index file imports every tool module and loops over them to call server.tool, so adding a new tool never means touching a five hundred line file again.
Adding a new tool is now a two step, entirely predictable change, create the new file, then add one import and one entry to the allTools array.
13. Naming Tools Consistently Across a Growing Server
As the tool count grows, naming discipline stops being a nice to have and starts being what keeps the tool list scannable for both humans and models.

blocks.text: 14. Testing That a Tool Shows Up Correctly in tools/list

blocks.alt: Testing That a Tool Shows Up Correctly in tools/list
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-949246968.png
The first test for any newly registered tool is the simplest one, call tools/list and check the entry looks exactly like what you intended to register.
If the name is misspelled, the description is missing, or a required field silently vanished, this is where you catch it, long before any model ever tries to call the tool.
15. Testing That a Tool Runs Correctly via tools/call
Discovery passing is not enough, the second test sends an actual tools/call request and checks the handler produces the right result.
A good habit is also calling tools/call with a deliberately invalid argument, like an empty city, and confirming the failure comes back as a clear error rather than a crash.
16. Versioning a Tool as Its Schema Changes

blocks.alt: Versioning a Tool as Its Schema Changes
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441012146-132278460.png
Tools rarely stay exactly the same forever, a field gets added, a field becomes required, or a whole tool gets replaced by a better one.
When a change would break existing callers, the safer path is usually to register a new tool name alongside the old one for a while, rather than silently changing what an existing name expects.
Once callers have moved over, the old tool can be removed from the registry cleanly, without ever having broken a call that used to work.
Worked Example
Say you are adding a new tool called add_task to a small productivity server. Start by writing the schema and handler together in one file.

Then register it by adding one import and one entry to the central tools array, run tools/list to confirm the schema looks right, then run tools/call with a real title to confirm the handler actually creates a task.
Common Mistakes

items: Renaming a field in the schema without renaming the matching destructured variable in the handler, leaving the handler silently reading undefined.
Adding a new required field to the schema without checking every existing example or test still sends it.
Piling every tool into one huge file until nobody wants to open it or safely add a new tool.
Skipping a tools/call test entirely and only ever checking that tools/list looks correct.
Letting a handler throw an unhandled exception instead of returning a clear isError result.
Giving two different tools nearly identical names, which confuses a model choosing between them.

blocks.text: Practice
Design and register a tool called cancel_reservation. It should require a reservation id, and optionally accept a cancellation reason.
Once written, check it against both tests from this lesson, confirm the schema is correct in tools/list, then confirm a real tools/call actually cancels a reservation.
Key Takeaway

Registering a tool means giving the SDK a name, a description, a schema, and a handler all at once, and those four pieces only stay trustworthy if they change together instead of drifting apart over time.

Splitting tools into their own files with one central registry keeps a growing server readable, and testing both tools/list and tools/call, not just one, is what actually proves a registered tool works.
